blocks.text: The molecular orbital approach explains the results of quantum mechanical calculations for covalent bonding. Its postulates are as follows.

items: During the formation of a molecule the atomic orbitals of the combining atoms overlap to form new orbitals called molecular orbitals, which belong to the whole molecule.
The atomic orbitals overlap with the lobe having the suitable sign of the wave function; one lobe of a p orbital is given the + sign and the other the - sign.

Two atomic orbitals overlap to form two molecular orbitals. When orbitals of the same sign overlap, a bonding molecular orbital (sigma or pi) forms, with lower energy than the parent atomic orbitals; with opposite signs a high-energy antibonding molecular orbital (sigma* or pi*) forms, with higher energy than the parent atomic orbitals.

The number of bonds between two atoms after the overlap is the bond order, taken as half the difference between the number of bonding electrons (a) and antibonding electrons (b): bond order = (a - b) / 2.

blocks.text: In the formation of H2 two s orbitals combine to give two molecular orbitals. The bonding molecular orbital sigma 1s is symmetrical about the axis joining the nuclei (the nuclear axis), while the antibonding orbital sigma* 1s has its electron density away from the nuclei of the overlapping atoms.

Head-on approach: the p orbitals of the two atoms approach along the same axis (say the x axis), giving the sigma 2px bonding and sigma* 2px antibonding molecular orbitals. Sideways approach: when the axes of two p orbitals (py or pz) are parallel they interact to form pi molecular orbitals. The bonding orbitals pi 2py and pi 2pz have zero electron density on the nuclear axis, which is a nodal plane, while the antibonding pi* 2py and pi* 2pz have the least electron density in the internuclear region.

blocks.alt: Left: two s orbitals of the same sign merge into a green bonding orbital between the nuclei, and two of opposite sign give a red antibonding orbital with a node. Middle: p orbitals meeting head-on for sigma and side by side for pi. Right: an energy level diagram for He2 with two electrons in sigma 1s and two in sigma* 1s. Below: level diagrams of the 2p molecular orbitals of N2, with six electrons in the bonding levels, and O2, with two unpaired electrons in pi* levels.
blocks.caption: Bonding and antibonding molecular orbitals, and the molecular orbital diagrams of He2, N2 and O2 (original diagram after Figures 3.34 to 3.38).
blocks.long_description: Two atomic orbitals always give two molecular orbitals: a bonding one, lower in energy with density between the nuclei, and an antibonding one, higher in energy with a node between them. Head-on p overlap gives sigma and sigma* orbitals; sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals gives pi and pi* orbitals with the nuclear axis as a nodal plane. He2 puts two electrons in sigma 1s and two in sigma* 1s, bond order zero, so no molecule. N2 fills pi 2py, pi 2pz and sigma 2px with six electrons, bond order three. O2 adds two more electrons singly into pi* 2py and pi* 2pz, bond order two and two unpaired electrons, so oxygen is paramagnetic.

blocks.prompt: Two atomic orbitals combine to give exactly two molecular orbitals. Describe the two, and say where the electrons of a bonding pi orbital are found.
blocks.explanation: One is the bonding orbital, formed when lobes of the same sign overlap; it lies lower in energy than the atomic orbitals and concentrates electron density between the nuclei. The other is the antibonding orbital, formed when lobes of opposite sign meet; it lies higher in energy and has a node, with density pushed away from the internuclear region. In a bonding pi orbital the density lies above and below the nuclear axis, which is itself a nodal plane with zero density.

items: MOT: atomic orbitals overlap to give molecular orbitals of the whole molecule; same-sign overlap gives a bonding orbital (sigma, pi, lower energy), opposite-sign overlap an antibonding orbital (sigma*, pi*, higher energy); bond order = (bonding - antibonding electrons) / 2.
s-s gives sigma 1s and sigma* 1s; head-on p gives sigma 2px and sigma* 2px; sideways p gives pi 2py, pi 2pz (nodal plane on the axis) and pi* 2py, pi* 2pz.
